acts.title: How a story goes viral
text: The internet has ___ the news industry in about two decades.

tts: Did you see that story about the Mexican woman who has just turned 127? — 127? Seriously? — Yes, she is the oldest person who has ever lived, apparently. According to the article, she claims she was born in 1887.

So she must have lived through a few interesting historical events. — I know. And it says in the article I read that she has something like seventy-three great-grandchildren and fifty-five great-great-grandchildren.

Apparently, although her physical health is not that great, she is mentally aware and still tells incredible stories of the Mexican Revolution. — So is she in the Guinness Book of Records? — Apparently not, because she has no proof of her age. She claims she lost her birth certificate while moving house forty years ago.

Did you read about the man who ran a marathon in a diving suit? Not a modern one — one of those old-fashioned ones from the 1940s, weighing around fifty-nine kilos. It took him six days, supposedly. From what it said in the article, he is quite well known for charity marathons in costume.

acts.title: Going Viral
tts: Welcome to Fleet Street, the traditional home of the British media. In 1702 London’s first daily newspaper was published near here, and for almost three hundred years this area was the centre of the UK’s newspaper industry.

For centuries most people in the UK got their news from newspapers. At the industry’s height, popular tabloids like the Sun and the Daily Mirror had a circulation of around four million. Today the Sun’s circulation is less than two million, and the Daily Mirror’s is less than one.

Millions of people across the world read news websites instead. Yahoo News, the world’s most-read news website, has an incredible one hundred and seventy-five million readers a month. And now social media sites are changing everything. In the USA, sixty-four per cent of adults use Facebook, and thirty per cent of those people reported that they read most of their news on the site.

But there are problems. Many social media users are not journalists, and some of these stories are not news at all. It is a vicious circle where newspapers report stories, those stories are shared and exaggerated online, and then other newspapers report from social media.

Look at this headline: “Ghost ship carrying cannibal rats heading for Britain.” Sounds terrifying. But the story was hugely overstated. The ship never came near British soil and there was no proof of rats being on board — certainly not cannibal rats.

items.q: What has happened to newspaper circulation?
o: It has fallen sharply — the Sun from four million to under two

items.q: What does the video call a “vicious circle”?
o: Papers report, stories are exaggerated online, then papers report the exaggeration

items.q: What was wrong with the cannibal rats story?
o: It was hugely overstated, and there was no proof of rats at all

items.q: What proportion of US adults use Facebook, according to the video?

acts.title: Going Viral
tts: London’s first daily newspaper, the Daily Courant, was published in 1702.

On the twenty-first of October 2013 the Irish Independent reported that an old Yugoslavian ship called the Lyubov Orlova had become loose and had gone missing in the Atlantic Ocean. The Irish Coast Guard director told the newspaper that the boat had been beside the harbour, so he assumed there were rats on board.

A few months later the Sun picked up the story. They interviewed a Belgian salvage dealer who wanted to find the ship to make money. He claimed there would be lots of rats and that rats eat each other.

The ship even got a Facebook page and a Twitter account. Many major newspapers reported the story and in the end had to admit that very little had happened. An animal expert pointed out that rats are as likely to eat one another as humans are.

acts.title: Retelling something you did not see
rule: Almost everything you tell somebody about the world you got from somewhere else. English has a set of markers for saying so, and using them is not weakness — it is the difference between reporting and inventing. The video in this lesson is a case study in what happens when they are dropped.
points: According to the article… It says in the article that… From what I read,…
Apparently, … Supposedly, … Allegedly, … The last is the strongest and is used where a legal claim is involved.
Attributing the claim to the speaker
She claims she was born in 1887. claim signals that you are not vouching for it.
Apparently and supposedly can open the sentence or close it. Allegedly usually sits before the verb.
Every step of the rat story removed one marker. By the fourth retelling, an assumption had become a fact.
eg: According to the article, she was born in 1887.
Names the source.
It says in the article that she has seventy-three great-grandchildren.
The same, less formal.
From what I read, he does this for charity.
Marks the limit of your knowledge.
Apparently, she is still mentally sharp.
Unverified, neutral.
It took him six days, supposedly.
Unverified, slightly sceptical.
He allegedly took the money.
Unverified, and legally careful.
She claims she lost the certificate.
The claim is hers, not yours.
The Coast Guard director assumed there were rats on board.
Reports the assumption as an assumption.
The story was hugely overstated.
What happens when nobody does the above.
An expert pointed out that rats rarely eat each other.
A named source correcting an unnamed one.
acts.careful: Apparently at the end of a sentence often carries a note of doubt in speech; at the beginning it is neutral. If you mean to be neutral, put it first.

write.q: Write a formal opinion essay of about 220 words on whether social media has made the news better or worse. State the question, give the strongest argument on each side with a concrete example, and reach a conclusion. Use at least three source markers or reporting verbs, and do not use “I think” more than once.
plan: the question, and what the essay will do
the case that it has improved things
the case that it has not
write.model:
Since about 2010 most people under forty have got their news from a feed rather than a front page, and the argument about whether this is an improvement has not moved on much. This essay considers both sides.

It could be argued that the change has been good. Events that would once have gone unreported are now captured within minutes by whoever is standing there, and a police shooting or a collapsing building no longer depends on a reporter arriving in time. According to the Reuters Institute, a majority of readers under thirty-five now encounter more sources in a week than their parents did in a year.

However, the counter-argument is stronger than it first appears. The problem is not that social media spreads false stories; it is that it spreads unhedged ones. A story about an abandoned ship in the Atlantic began as a coastguard official saying he assumed there were rats on board. Four retellings later, national newspapers reported that cannibal rats were heading for Britain. Nobody lied. Everybody simply removed one qualification.

In conclusion, the technology has widened access and narrowed care. What has been lost is not accuracy but the habit of saying how sure you are, and that habit is what made the accuracy checkable.
